#6299. The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

The days of needing jumper cables and another motorist to revive your vehicle are over.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

Like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

There are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can quickly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

With 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

This device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—important so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

Protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

The interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review

This is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

It has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

The Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.)

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

For motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

With 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

For years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

With 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

Portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

The two most important specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

If you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two important. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will issue a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That said, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

#6298. Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A tight bend in the subducting Pacific plate may help explain Challenger Deep

The ROV Jason/Medea (Jason shown here during a 2021 dive at the East Pacific Rise) can descend up to 6,500 meters below the ocean surface. In a new study, it helped researchers discover volcanic deposits in the Mariana Trench.

D. Fornari, WHOI-SSSG, MISO Facility, NDSF Jason Team, NSF

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

November's full Beaver Moon rises on Tuesday, Nov. 24, giving us a preview of the spectacular Christmas Eve supermoon coming next month.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Tuesday (Nov. 24) to indicate that the full Beaver Moon rises tonight.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk tonight (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. #6296. Scientists Figured Out How to Rewire Your Brain—Literally

Hope for depression, autism, and neurodegeneration: Plug in new wires instead of fixing broken ones.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The brain is a wondrous organ that’s so complex it’s often referred to as a computer, complete with electrical wiring in the forms of neurons, synapses, and axons. However, unlike computers, there’s no easy way to deftly repair faulty wiring, especially down at the cellular level. For decades, the best tools at a physician's disposal for tackling serious neurological diseases were medications or, in more dire scenarios, external therapies such as deep brain stimulation.

Those treatments can bring real relief, but they don’t fix the underlying problem. But if the brain really runs on electrical connections, shouldn’t it be possible to route signals around damaged areas by rewiring specific neurons? A team of U.S. researchers led by Kafui Dzirasa of Duke University School of Medicine thinks so. In May, they described a new technology called “LinCx” in the journal Nature. It uses engineered versions of proteins found in fish that naturally form electrical synapses, and it can link two specifically chosen neurons.

“For decades, neuroscience has lacked tools that can precisely control communication between specific cell types,” Dzirasa, the senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “By introducing a way to plug in new electrical connections with cellular‑level precision, our study marks a major step forward in the ability to edit brain circuitry and understand how neural networks give rise to behavior.”

The system relies on structures called “gap junctions.” Each one is made of two hemichannels, and each hemichannel is built from six proteins called connexins. Through these gap junctions, cells exchange chemical and electrical signals, but they usually form unpredictably across cells. The innovation of the LinCx system is that it uses modified proteins that dock with one another while ignoring native brain proteins.

“The goal sounded almost simple: Make two proteins connect only to each other,” Carnegie Mellon’s Elizabeth Ransey, former Duke University postdoctoral researcher and lead author, said in a separate press statement. “We can specify both sides of the connection. That gives us much more precision than approaches that activate one population and indirectly affect everything downstream.”

The team tested the system in simple structures, such as human-derived cells and frog oocytes, and eventually moved on to more complex ones. Previous studies have rewired the neural circuits of Caenorhabditis elegans, a species of nematode commonly used in neurobiology. However, using the technology on mammals, specifically laboratory mice, was a first. In both worms and mice, the scientists noted changing behavior after performing this “neural bypass.” C. elegans, for example, modified its temperature-seeking behavior, and mice altered targeted responses to social interaction and stress.

By focusing on bypassing damaged areas rather than repairing them, physicians could provide improved brain function in those experiencing depression, autism, and many types of neurodegenerative disease.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6295. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

#6293. ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Big Dig podcast host Ian Coss explores how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy worked together to reform American health care laws

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”

#6292. A Blind Woman Mastered Echolocation in Just 10 Weeks—And You Can Learn This Superpower Too, Scientists Say

You have the capacity to alter your perceptual reality in an astonishingly short period of time.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed. Mid-conversation, her friend interrupted and said, “Oh, that was fascinating. You just avoided a van without realizing you’d done it.”

This amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind. She had used echolocation to detect the van, which was parked on the sidewalk, and navigated around it without even noticing. “I wasn’t consciously thinking about what I was doing at the time. Instead, I was naturally using echolocation, picking up changes in the way sound reflected from the vehicle and using that information to navigate around the obstacle,” says Hyde-Dryden, a rehabilitation teacher in the UK. Like many blind echolocators, she creates a sharp, quick sound by clicking her tongue and then listens for the echo.

While echolocation comes easily to her now, Hyde-Dryden had to work hard to learn it. Almost 20 years ago, while she was losing her sight to glaucoma, she attended a short workshop and spent hours practicing the clicking technique she learned there. But she didn’t feel confident using it until 2019 when she signed up for an intensive echolocation study at Durham University.

That study was spearheaded by Lore Thaler, PhD, a neuroscientist at Durham University whose work over the last 15 years has uncovered how echolocation changes the brain. Her research goes beyond studying the variability of perception between people, and highlights just how much one person’s perceptual reality can change, even in a short timeframe.

Thaler started her research journey studying visual perception, but her work took an unexpected turn when a collaborator introduced her to a blind echolocator. At the time, she hadn’t heard of human echolocation, but “the way he described the world was very easy to relate to from a sighted person’s perspective,” she says.

After diving into the literature, Thaler found scattered and disjointed research on echolocation, and “very little was known about the brain basis of it,” she says. “That’s where we came in.”

She and her collaborators used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to track two blind participants’ brain activity while they listened to recordings of their own echolocation clicks and echoes.

The auditory cortex responded more to echoes than non-echoes in both participants but so did regions of their visual cortex, including areas associated with visual shape perception. Even though this was what she had hoped to find, actually seeing it “was a wonderful surprise,” says Thaler, leading to “a great feeling of discovery.” When she and her team submitted the paper in 2011, the findings were contentious—so contentious that the journal they submitted to asked double the typical number of reviewers to take a look at it. Some thought it was an incredible finding; others thought it was predictable. But in the end, the paper got published, and when it did, it made a huge splash in the neuroscience community.

The project shifted the way Thaler’s collaborators, and later many in the field, thought about the visual cortex. Perhaps the “visual cortex” was a misleading term, some experts thought. Instead, “maybe it’s a thing for processing spatial information,” says Melvyn Goodale, PhD, a neuroscientist at Western University and Thaler’s collaborator on the project.

After that first study on echolocation, Thaler was hooked. She launched an entire lab of her own at Durham University dedicated to human echolocation research. She went on to study how echolocators perceive motion, navigate new spaces, and distinguish between textures like velvet or glass.

By the time Hyde-Dryden made her way to Durham in 2019, Thaler was embarking on her most ambitious project yet: a 10-week echolocation training program for both blind and sighted people.

Each two-hour training session involved a slew of tasks. One involved standing in front of two foam discs and deciding which was larger. Another required participants to navigate through a virtual maze with recorded clicks and echoes. During every session, participants also explored an indoor or outdoor space with the help of Thaler or one of her collaborators to practice echolocating in the real world. Thaler even brought Hyde-Dryden to the Newcastle train station to help her learn the intricacies of echolocating in a busy, loud environment. Over time, Hyde-Dryden built up a mental “library of echo patterns” for familiar objects.

Both blind and sighted participants improved substantially at each of these tasks over the course of the 10 weeks. Just as in the initial 2011 paper and many of her follow-up studies, Thaler also wanted to understand brain activity during echolocation. This time, she had participants hop in the MRI machine both before and after learning to echolocate.

Before the study, Hyde-Dryden had heard from an expert blind echolocator that being inside of the MRI would feel tight and uncomfortable, but when she went into the MRI before the echolocation training, it didn’t bother her at all. After the training, however, the MRI felt quite different. “When I went in at the end, I felt horrendous. I felt ill afterwards. I felt really sick. And I think it was because I was more aware.”

Those fMRI scans revealed that participants’ brains became attuned to echoes, whether or not they were blind. Echoes elicited a larger response in both the auditory cortex and in the primary visual cortex.

“It paired I think nicely with what we, up to that point, had only been able to show in these expert echolocators,” Thaler says. But it pushed the findings even further, demonstrating that participants don’t need to be blind to have malleable visual cortices. After just 10 weeks of training, the visual cortex becomes attuned to sounds that carry information about space. And other labs have shown that sighted people don’t even need to learn echolocation to retrain their visual cortex; a few days with a blindfold can tune your visual cortex to sound and touch signals it wouldn’t normally process.

Since that training, Hyde-Dryden has started to use echolocation every day. “It really was an absolute game changer for me,” she says. Thanks to echolocation, when her daughter was young, Hyde-Dryden was able to use both hands to scoop her up from the bath, bringing her into the bedroom without having to hold a cane at the same time. In conjunction with her cane and guide dog, echolocation has made Hyde-Dryden feel much more confident navigating new spaces. Even in busy train stations with high ceilings where the echo can get lost, she can find her way without assistance.

Despite success stories like hers, “it’s not a skill that is widely taught anywhere in the world,” Hyde-Dryden says. Echolocation is taught by a small number of people and is sometimes loosely included in rehabilitation curricula, “but it is certainly not given the emphasis that it should.”

Thaler hopes to change that. She has offered free workshops for years and, this year, she plans to give training sessions to more than 100 rehabilitation professionals at Guide Dogs UK who will then train their hundreds of clients.

“I think the neuroscience stuff has been a good vehicle to drive home the message ‘this is real, this has to be taken seriously,’” says Thaler. “But then to actually go out and do the training and make it useful for people, of course, that’s still another step.”

Nora Bradford is a cognitive scientist and science journalist. During her Ph.D., she investigated metacognition, or “thinking about thinking.” That research echoes throughout her science writing, as she typically covers perception, cognition, and learning across human and non-human animals. You can find her words in Scientific American, National Geographic, Quanta Magazine, and Science News, as well as in video-form on SciShow and PBS Terra. Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. #6290. The 8 Best Headphones for Giving Your Ears the Treatment They Deserve

Our handpicked, tested sets start at around $100.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The fact of the matter is that it doesn’t take a lot of work to find a good pair of headphones these days. After decades of competition and high-tech design, the market is saturated with dozens of high-quality options at every shape, size, and price point. Whether you’re looking for a basic set of earbuds for less than $100, or would prefer to drop $300 to $500 on a pair of wireless ANC headphones with high-tech bells and whistles like support for lossless audio files, or even want to spend top-dollar on a pair of wired, audiophile-grade cans to plug into an immaculately constructed hi-fi system, you won’t be short on choices.

Over the past five years or so, there haven’t been many game-changing innovations in the audio space, but that has led to a flattening of the field that’s great if you’re looking for a bargain. Features that would have once been considered high-end, like active noise cancellation, have trickled down into budget products, and audio quality has been steadily improving among budget- and mid-tier headphones. There are benefits to buying a high-end pair, for sure, but there are more bargains than ever before.

Obviously there are hundreds, if not thousands, of headphones out there—more than even I can test. I’ve put in a lot of time, though, going over the best, the most interesting, and the most talked about headphones, to find the ones that stand out from the pack. Because even when there are a lot of good options out there, we all would rather bring home the best.

I’ve been professionally testing tech products and audio gear, especially headphones and earbuds, since 2011. When I evaluate headphones, I spend weeks and, in some cases, months using each product as my daily driver, assessing its sound, battery life, and ergonomics. I pair the headsets with phones and laptops and frequently switch between devices.

My test routine included streaming an eclectic selection of tracks from Apple Music and Qobuz to evaluate each headset's ability to produce audible bass, treble, and mid-range. I also listened to podcasts, streamed videos, and played video games while evaluating each pair of headphones.

To put the headphones’ noise cancellation through its paces, I wear them on the New York City subway to get to work, in the large open office I share with my colleagues, and on long-distance flights. I make calls, too, carefully observing if their microphones help participants hear me clearly.

I monitor the battery performance of all wireless headphones by tracking how often I have to charge them. I want to ensure that every pick’s battery life at least matches its manufacturer’s claims.

Because you may wear your headphones for long stretches each day, I carefully scrutinize the size, fit, and ergonomics of every pair by using them for hours between breaks. I also evaluate the layout and reliability of their controls, whether they are buttons, touch-sensitive surfaces, or a combination of both.

With that guidance in mind, find your next favorite pair of headphones among the thoroughly tested and reviewed sets below.

If I had to part with all my headphones and keep just one pair, I’d choose the Technics A1000. These wireless headphones are my new benchmark for all-around excellence, blending an elegant yet understated design, supreme comfort, and outstanding audio performance. That includes high-fidelity sound and efficient noise cancellation on par with the industry’s best offerings.

Featuring sophisticated magnetic-fluid audio drivers, the Technics A1000 headphones impressed me with balanced, detail-rich, distortion-free sound right out of the box, faithfully reproducing everything I listened to during testing — from music and podcasts to video content. Instrumentals in my eclectic jazz selection sounded crisp and vibrant. On my favorite downtempo albums, the bass was deep, while the vocals were superbly defined and perfectly separated.

The Technics companion app gave me a rich set of tools to customize the headphones’ sound and noise cancellation. Depending on the music I was listening to, I could adjust the bass and treble levels and tweak the mid-range output to my liking, using a graphic equalizer or pre-loaded presets.

In a mandatory comparison with identically-priced rivals like the Sony WH-1000XM6 and the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) — a duo of products with superior button controls, longer battery life, more futureproof Bluetooth 6.0 connectivity with the ability to simultaneously link to three devices, and full Dolby Atmos audio capabilities with optional head tracking. The last point is a step above Sony’s proprietary, multidimensional 360 Reality Audio, which is more cumbersome to access.

We’ve reached a point where a pair of wireless headphones from a reputable brand with elegant design, high-quality sound (including spatial audio), stellar noise cancellation, and long battery life costs over $400. By offering some of these features for $200, the Nothing Headphone (a) over-ear cans are the biggest bang for the buck and worth the attention of value-obsessed gearheads.

Design- and durability-wise, the Nothing Headphone (a) makes similarly priced rivals look generic by comparison. The headphones’ rectangular ear cups with rounded corners give them the same distinctive look as pricier offerings from the same maker. These include transparent and solid-color bits that give the headset unique character. Their IP52 water- and dust-resistance rating is also remarkable, as it’s rare for over-ear headphones at any price point.

Amazing hardware button controls that include roller and paddle keys, as well as a customizable one, are another reason I became a fan of the Nothing Headphone (a) and all other headsets from the brand. Their responsiveness and tactility are better than products that cost twice as much.

On the audio front, the headphones delivered enjoyable, slightly bass-forward sound and immersive spatial audio. The Nothing X app offered intuitive tools to customize my listening experience, and I liked the option to link the cans directly to my devices via a USB-C or a standard audio cable. The cans’ noise cancellation was also solid, if not on par with the serenity offered by more expensive competitors.

The 75-hour maximum battery life with noise cancellation alone is reason enough to put the Nothing Headphone (a) on your radar. I didn’t have to worry about recharging the headset for weeks. Turning noise cancellation off almost doubles the battery life, bringing it to a staggering 135 hours between charges.

Bose headphones and earbuds have been synonymous with noise-canceling excellence for decades, so it’s no surprise the brand’s QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) over-ear cans are the first product that comes to mind if this feature is a priority. Of course, the headphones are also stylish, supremely comfortable, and deliver top-notch sound, including immersive spatial audio.

Regarding noise cancellation, I wouldn’t recommend the headphones solely for their ability to eliminate ambient noise distractions quickly, since that’s a given in this price range. What gives the Bose product an edge over any rival in this department is the option to customize the noise cancellation by choosing from eleven levels of intensity, then saving it into a custom mode for specific activities (e.g., work, travel, commuting, etc.) that’s easy to access by long-pressing a button.

Having a quick-access mode with maxed-out noise cancellation for work and travel, another where the feature’s intensity was set below 50% for my daily subway rides, and one with full ambient awareness at the tip of my right thumb was super convenient with the Bose headphones. Plus, I could include spatial audio in my custom modes.

During months of use, the QuietComfort Ultra headphones delivered powerful, entertaining sound, customizable via their companion app. Their spatial audio capabilities are just as impressive, and I tip my hat to Bose for making proprietary Immersive Audio technology, with or without dynamic head tracking, available on any content, not just Dolby Atmos-enhanced music and videos. That said, if audio fidelity is your top priority, you’ll likely prefer the identically priced Technics EAH-A1000 or the Sony WH-1000XM6.

Calls sound superb on the QC Ultra 2, as usual. I like the headphones’ control layout, with clicky buttons and a volume touch slider that doubles as a customizable key. The QuietComfort Ultra’s 30-hour battery life with noise cancellation is far from best-in-class, but ahead of the previous version and more than enough to keep you tranquil on any flight.

We live in times when most consumers think of headphones as bulky over-ear headsets, and that’s what makes the Marshall Milton ANC special. These headphones offer features and performance you’d expect from a larger set—top-notch sound customizable via an app, reliable noise cancellation, and long battery life—in a more compact, lightweight package with an on-ear fit and scratch-resistant ear cup covers better suited to on-the-go use.

Sound-wise, the Marshall Milton ANC impressed me with crisp, energetic sound that you can customize via a companion app. Its noise cancellation is also stellar, though the headset doesn't deliver the same level of tranquility as a top-shelf over-ear pair. The extra layer of passive noise isolation such headsets provide is instrumental. Still, the Milton ANC makes up for it with a lighter and more comfortable fit.

The headphones’ knob and customizable button are excellent and miles ahead of many competitors’ control layouts. So is their 80-hour maximum battery life without noise cancellation. If you like the Milton ANC’s design and controls, but want an over-ear set, I have good news. The Marshall Monitor III ANC headphones offer similar design and controls in an over-ear form factor with a slightly higher price tag.

Review: Marshall Milton ANC Wireless Headphones

The Soundcore Q31i wireless headphones by Anker are your best bet if you want to stay in two-digit price territory. Believe it or not, for under $100, you can get a reliable set with a comfy fit, solid audio performance, good noise cancellation for the price, futureproof connectivity, and price-defying battery life in a choice of three colors (black, white, and pink).

Acoustically, the Soundcore Q31i headphones performed better than their price tag suggests. The sound was surprisingly harmonious out of the box and customizable via the feature-packed app. While I wouldn’t ditch my expensive headphones for the Anker offering, I found its sound super enjoyable. Their support for Hi-Res audio in wired and wireless mode was a particularly nice touch that felt unthinkable at this price point.

The headphones’ noise cancellation is adequate, if far from the best in the business. I didn’t get the same silence as with more expensive products, but I had no trouble focusing at our large open office when I put the headphones on. The key feature, like the sound, is adjustable in the companion app.

Overall, the Soundcore Q31i exceeded my expectations when I put it through its paces. The lack of spatial audio is my only gripe with the headset, but at $60 on sale, it’s nowhere near a dealbreaker.

Audio-Technica’s ATH-M50x is the first option that comes to mind when someone asks me to recommend a pair of wired over-ear headphones that offer top-notch sound, commendable ergonomics, and impeccable brand cachet, all at an agreeable price. The legendary maker’s product ticks all these boxes, so whether you are looking to take a break from Bluetooth or need a reliable tool for work, or to enjoy, say, your vinyl collection, it is an excellent buy.

A consistently balanced, high-fidelity sound is among the many reasons why many audio engineers and audiophiles swear by these Audio-Technica headphones. My favorite aspect of their audio performance is its accurate and enjoyable bass depth. Countless wired and wireless headphones, especially in this price range, are heavy on bass but nowhere near as proficient in producing mid-range and highs, which is why I always keep the ATH-M50x in my rotation.

The headphones’ retail package is as rich as their sound. It includes three cables of various lengths and a soft pouch. Due to their immense (and well-deserved) popularity among consumers, Audio-Technica ATH-M50x headphones have an excellent ecosystem of third-party cables, cases, and ear cup covers.

If what I told you about the ATH-M50x piqued your interest, but you prefer wireless headphones, I have good news. Audio-Technica offers a Bluetooth version of the cans. The Audio-Technica ATH-M20x headphones, on the other hand, are a great option for upgraders on a very tight budget.

The Technics EAH-AZ100 wireless earbuds offer the same blend of acoustic excellence and onboard features as the brand’s over-ear headphones I mentioned, but in a sleeker, lighter package with an in-ear fit and a lower price tag. These qualities make the buds my top pick in their crowded product category. I’d take the Technics offering as my sole set of earbuds over any big-name rival.

Equipped with magnetic-fluid audio drivers, the EAH-AZ100 delivered pristine, distortion-free sound across countless listening sessions. The harmony among bass, mid-range, and treble fully met my high expectations. The buds’ spatial audio output, with full Dolby Atmos support and optional head tracking, was equally impressive. Their call performance was also stellar.

The earphones’ ability to tune out ambient noise matches their audio fidelity and is rightfully among the industry’s best. Thanks to passive noise isolation from their comfortable ear tips and sophisticated hardware, I had no trouble blocking out distractions when I needed to. The companion app let me choose between fully adaptive noise cancellation based on my surroundings or a desired level of noise cancellation.

Like the Technics over-ear headphones, I compared the EAH-AZ100 buds with their direct competitors: the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) and the Sony WF-1000XM6. In this group of elite options, the Technics set earned my nod for offering (arguably) better Dolby Atmos-certified sound, longer battery life, and simultaneous connection to three devices. Noise cancellation is equally great across all products, though I’d give Bose an edge for offering custom settings for specific scenarios. Lastly, this might sound like nitpicking, but the EAH-AZ100’s charging case is sleeker and fits more easily in the small pocket of my jeans than its rivals’.

Bowers & Wilkins has sterling credibility among discerning audiophiles — the folks who obsess over high-fidelity stereo sound with precise separation between left and right channels and are willing to spend big on gear that delivers it. The British audio maker’s Px8 S2 wireless headphones should top the wish list for this group of gearheads, offering a listening experience similar to its luxury speakers in a pair of over-ear headphones.

Listening to the Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2 headphones felt like being in a private space with a hi-fi system. Their out-of-the-box stereo sound captivated me with its accurate presentation, as intended by the content’s audio engineers. Depending on the song and genre, I could hear lively vocals, crisp instrumentals, and deep bass without opening the companion app to tweak settings. By contrast, their strong noise cancellation put me in a cocoon of silence, letting me focus solely on the music.

Of course, the Bowers & Wilkins app gave me plenty of options to customize the cans’ sound and even activate an immersive spatial audio mode. However, I liked the original sound so much that I kept it as-is most of the time, whether wired or Bluetooth.

In a manner befitting their price category and brand heritage, the Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2 deliver style and craftsmanship in spades. The headphones are made from a mix of leather, metal, and fabric, so they look and feel luxurious. Their comfort and button controls are equally impressive, fully meeting my lofty expectations after months of testing.

Before we dig into hardware specs and features to keep on your radar, know that spending more on your next Bluetooth or wired headset will get you better audio performance across the board and more onboard features. By audio performance, I mean noise cancellation, support for immersive spatial audio, and superior call quality, among other essentials. These features require sophisticated onboard processors and multiple integrated microphones, which inevitably reflects the retail price.

Many budget cans support lossless audio formats, but you shouldn’t prioritize this unless you have a top-shelf Android phone that supports audiophile-grade LDAC and Qualcomm AptX codecs. Lossless audio also isn't available on Spotify, so make sure your streaming service supports it. Apple Music, Amazon Music, Tidal, and Qobuz are a few that do.

If you’re shopping on a tight budget, I suggest spending $80 to $100 for a good pair. The most feature-packed wireless noise-canceling headphones cost north of $400, so budget accordingly if you want one. You’ll find your investment well worth it when you turn on noise canceling and discover it’s like a mute button for your surroundings.

Due to their lack of Bluetooth chips, batteries, and additional components to control noise cancellation, spatial audio, and other features, wired headphones can treat you to better stereo sound quality than equivalently priced Bluetooth models. Their makers can use more capable, better-tuned audio drivers while keeping the price reasonable without those extra bits, so you can score a high-quality pair from a big-name brand for less than $200.

On the other hand, if ultimate high-fidelity and craftsmanship are priorities for you, prepare to spend a hefty four-digit sum to get what you need. Paired with an amplifier and lossless streaming, high-end wired headphones can help you (literally) discover new tones and layers in songs and albums you’ve listened to hundreds of times before. To be clear, though, only the most dedicated audiophiles should even consider something like that.

The headphones’ audio drivers deliver sound to your ears. The materials used in their making and their tuning are more important than their size. Translation? More expensive headphones feature more sophisticated drivers, resulting in higher-quality sound with a more palpable balance between bass, treble, and mid-range.

After more than a decade of headphone testing, I can confirm that cheaper models often hide their sonic deficiencies behind heavier bass. A booming low end can affect treble and mid-range production, reducing the quality of the sonic experience even if it still sounds entertaining.

Multi-dimensional spatial audio has become a standard feature on most high-end wireless headphones. By making the sound effects feel as if they come from distinct directions instead of just your left, right, and center, headphones with this lifelike functionality will make you feel like you are in the studio with the artist, part of the audience when streaming a live album, or in the onscreen action.

Better yet, the best wireless headphones with spatial audio have sophisticated onboard tech that can process standard audio into immersive multi-channel sound, including the option to add dynamic head tracking for a truly lifelike experience. As its name suggests, this feature shifts the sound source as you move your head for an even more natural listening experience.

This feature is a must for a new pair of wireless headphones in 2025—and you no longer have to pay top dollar for it. Once reserved for premium headsets, the functionality is available across the price spectrum, including under-$100 territory. It utilizes microphones and a processor integrated into the headphones to detect ambient sounds and then deliver audio that cancels those sound waves out.Noise cancellation will reduce auditory distractions during your commutes, travels, and workday. Don’t buy Bluetooth headphones that lack it, even if your budget is below $100. Naturally, spending $200 or more will give you superior noise cancellation, often resulting in near-total silence on top-shelf sets.

I typically suggest wireless headphones if you’re looking for an upgrade, not only for offering cable-free convenience but also for desirable features like noise cancellation, spatial audio, and app controls for customizing those. Look for wireless headphones with Bluetooth 5.2 (or higher) on board. These are the most futureproof wireless connectivity standards. Don’t worry if your device doesn’t support them. They are backward-compatible with older Bluetooth standards.

Wired headphones deserve your attention for their rock-solid connection to hardware, which provides instantaneous sound transmission with zero latency. Measured in milliseconds, latency is the time it takes for audio to reach wireless headphones from the source—your phone, tablet, or TV, for example. It’s imperceptible in most cases.That said, a zero-latency wired link can come in handy for video-editing projects, where the audio and on-screen content have to stay in perfect sync. The same goes for competitive gaming, where every millisecond counts.

Opting for a cable-toting set of headphones also frees you from charging, companion apps, and firmware updates. By lacking electronic components and degradable batteries, wired headsets also last longer.

Don’t settle for a wireless noise-canceling headset that can deliver less than 20 hours of battery life, as it might not be enough to get you through a super-long flight. The over- and on-ear sets I recommend here will last at least 30 hours between charges, and that’s my minimum requirement in 2026.

Still, since superior noise cancellation and fancy spatial audio tax the headphones’ battery, I didn’t mind charging the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra (Gen 2) to get a better experience than what their lower-priced rivals offered. The same goes for the Apple AirPods Max 2.

If you are shopping for wireless earbuds, a double-digit maximum battery life of at least 10 hours between charges from the bundled charging case is preferable, but not mandatory. Top-tier AirPods and Bose earphones can’t reach this milestone, but they are still easy to recommend for their excellence in other areas.

Except for AirPods and Beats by Dre products, which benefit from Apple’s superb hardware integration, any new pair of wireless headphones must come with a companion app. This includes Beats products, which can play nice with Android phones just as well as they do with an iPhone. It lets you control them and keep them up to date with firmware updates.

And look for a hard-shell storage case when shopping for Bluetooth headphones. It will keep them intact when you toss them in a bag or backpack on your way to work, or stuff them into a carry-on suitcase when traveling. No need to fret if your headphones come with a soft pouch for storage, though; just keep them at the top of your bag while packing to avoid potential (if highly unlikely) damage.

Stefan is an award-winning consumer technology editor with over a decade of experience in reviewing gadgets, particularly smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, desktop and laptop computers across multiple form factors and platforms, as well as accessories for them. He also covers televisions and audio equipment, including headphones, earbuds, wireless speakers, and soundbars. Since joining Hearst in 2015, Stefan has contributed to BestProducts, Popular Mechanics, and numerous other publications. Prior to his current role, he served as the US Editor for GSMArena.com.
