#6267. Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie said. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?"

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently."

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”

"Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

#6266. The 6 Best Electric Snowblowers Are Plenty Powerful—and Quieter Alternatives to Gas Models

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Two more reasons to go green: Battery-powered outdoor equipment is also easier to operate and store.

If you’re looking for the quickest, least labor-intensive way to dig out after a big snowstorm this winter, a snowblower is it. While it’s only fall, it’s not too early to think about getting a snowblower if you found yourself wanting one during last year’s winter storms but struggled to find a retailer that wasn’t already out of stock. Getting ahead of the game is a good idea.

Electric models are more capable than ever, and in some cases meet or exceed their gas-powered brethren in some respects. Cordless, battery-electric blowers can clear a path up to roughly 2 feet wide through as much as 20 inches of snow. They start with the push of a button, require less maintenance than gas machines, and run relatively quietly. They’re also easier to store than their gas-powered counterparts.

Ahead, we review both two-stage snow blowers and single-stage snow throwers and recommend models from Toro, Ego, Milwaukee, and more.

Our selections for this list are based on our years of testing snow blowers of all varieties. Most of these examples we’ve tested in the last few years, and others are updated versions of models we’ve tested. We are also planning for a substantial update to this guide in the coming weeks with new models.

Tony Carrick, the original author of this article, is a regular PopMech contributor and writes about everything from landscaping to home improvement. He grew up in rural Pennsylvania, where he became well-acquainted with blizzards and the backbreaking labor of digging out after them. His recommendations are based on his personal experience testing snow blowers at home, along with plenty of research to inform the picks. He compared specs for a variety of corded and cordless models, while also plowing through recommendations and feedback from dozens of customer reviews.

Ego Power+ 21-Inch Single-Stage Snow Blower

Ego claims this single-stage snow blower is able to clear a 14-car driveway on a single charge. Plus, it has heated handles.

Ryobi’s latest single-stage blower comes with two 40-volt, 8-amp-hour batteries for long runtime. It also has a tall clearing depth of 11.5 inches.

Wild Badger Power 20-Inch Single-Stage Snow Blower

We’re checking out this single-stage budget option to see if it can achieve effective snow removal for a small property.

This is Ego’s latest two-stage blower, which we’re evaluating to see if it can hold its own against a gas-powered two-stage snow blower.

Electric snow blowers may not be able to match the power of their gas-powered counterparts, but this self-propelled two-stage model from Ryobi comes close. It sports four rechargeable 40-volt 6-amp-hour batteries, which Ryobi claims can power the snow blower for up to 45 minutes, and move the same amount of snow as a 252-cc gas-powered two-stage snow blower. It has the power to scoop up a path that’s 24 inches wide and 21 inches deep, then chuck it up to 55 feet away.

We’re also impressed with the cockpit, which allows you to control the speed of the drive wheels and the auger, change the direction of the chute, and toggle the LED headlights without missing a beat. The handlebar even heats up so your hands don’t get numb as you're working.

Our only concern is with the charger. While we like the fact that this Ryobi supports rapid charging, the charger only has two slots, which means you’ll have to go through two rounds of recharging before you’re back to full power.

If you don’t relish the idea of pushing heavy machinery through heavy snow, Snow Joe makes a lightweight single-stage snow blower that’s fairly easy to push around. At less than 38 pounds with batteries installed, the Snow Joe 24V-X2-SB18 is easy to roll out of storage, push down the driveway, and maneuver through turns.

The scraper bar clears snow right down to the pavement, and it can launch snow up to 20 feet away. On top of that, it’s very cheap—one of the most affordable cordless snow blowers we’ve found.

Unsurprisingly, that light weight and low price come with some compromises. The 18-inch-wide chute cuts a narrow path, so you’ll need to take a few extra passes to get the job done right compared to a wider machine. Meanwhile, its two 24-volt batteries offer a modest 40-minute run time.

Combine those two things, and the 24V-X2-SB18 is best reserved for smaller jobs like clearing decks, walkways, and compact driveways. If that’s what you need, though, it makes snow removal cheap and easy.

We like Ego’s battery-powered outdoor equipment because it’s among the best when it comes to power and run time—and this two-stage snow blower is no exception. With its two 56-volt, 7.5-Ah batteries and 24-inch-wide intake, the Power+ SNT2405 can clear a 8-inch layer of snow from an 18-car driveway on a single charge.

We also like the cockpit on this self-propelled machine. You can change speeds while in forward or reverse, adjust the auger speed, and change the chute direction all without having to leave the controls. It also comes equipped with four bright LED headlights, useful in the event your snow clearing efforts take you past sundown.

We also like the fact that Ego uses mostly steel construction with this machine, so you can expect it to hold up for many a winter.

Ego claims its 21-inch Power+ snow blower can throw snow up to 40 feet with a 180-degree, adjustable chute, which is pretty far for a cordless machine. In the wet sawdust test, we were able to throw 24 feet with the heavier, denser material—longer distances are certainly achievable with lighter, drier snow. It took the Power+ 4 minutes 16 seconds to clear the sawdust down to pavement in our area test.

Like most single-stage blowers, the Power+ is not self-propelled, so we needed to push it into the snow. In our dense, heavy sawdust, that took some effort to make forward progress. It’s not a bad thing, though, as it makes it easier to prevent the machine from digging in too deep and bogging down. In very wet or ice-packed snow, we expect you’ll have to put in a similar effort.

The Power+ has a variable-speed auger, so we were able to adjust speed for the conditions and conserve battery when less power was needed. There isn’t too much to worry about in the battery department, since it comes with two 5-Ah batteries, enough to clear 8 inches of snow on a 12-car driveway—that’s six cars long by two cars wide.

The Power+ comes with a dual-port charger, so the two batteries can be charged simultaneously to get you ready for the next round faster. Ego rounds things out with front-mounted LEDs for low-light and dark conditions, plus an easy-folding handle for stowing the unit when not in use.

The 60-volt 26-inch Power Max e26 is one of the models we tested in November 2025, and it’s among the burliest two-stage cordless snow blowers we’ve used. It is built virtually the same as a gas model, except with an electric motor and two batteries. That includes the frame, drive system, auger, and auger housing.

Since it’s built the same, we can confirm it performs the same—so it could easily replace a similar gas model. No caveats here; the Power Max e26 isn’t a compromise in any significant way that we could determine. It comes with two batteries and a (claimed) runtime of up to 70 minutes—enough to clear a driveway 30 car spaces long.

Operating the Power Max e26 was a pleasant experience, if you can call snow blowing pleasant. It has effective heated hand grips, and an axle with a differential that allows you to turn quickly, on a dime—no having to muscle it around.

The e26 easily handled our testing with wet sawdust, throwing it far enough to cross an average driveway—even when making a full 26-inch-wide pass. If you’ve questioned whether a cordless snow blower could ever be as good as a gas machine, the e26 answers that affirmatively.

Milwaukee’s M18 single-stage snow blower is the second machine we tested in November 2025, and it also impressed us. It's noticeably heavier than many other similar cordless models, which seems to be due to its metal frame. At 90 pounds, it isn’t heavy, at least in comparison to two-stage machines, but the weight is an advantage, helping prevent the blower from bouncing around or riding up when encountering denser, crusty snow.

We tested this snow blower with wet sawdust, which always presents a little bit of a challenge with single-stage snow blowers, as they have to lift the snow and eject it in one operation. Milwaukee’s M18 blower did this well enough in testing—and if it can throw wet sawdust, it will really throw the snow.

To facilitate ejecting snow, the M18’s chute is wider than that of most other models. This eliminates potential bottlenecks and ultimately clogs, where the snow passes from the blower body into the chute. Milwaukee's single auger is edged with a rubber paddle that both sweeps the pavement clean and pulls the machine forward. It does this well enough that, in some instances, we had to hold it back a little in testing.

The chute has a remote adjustment—you can crank a knob just below the handlebar to change the direction of the chute, allowing you to put snow where it needs to go. However, ejection elevation is manually adjusted at the top of the chute—but this isn't something you typically need to adjust as often.

Milwaukee claims the M18 blower can clear up to 11 parking places, or 500 feet of sidewalk on the two included 12.0-Ah batteries. But with two extra battery ports, you can double the runtime by adding another pair of batteries. We’ll be testing this more as we have snow available.

There are two types of snow blowers for homeowners, based on the number of “stages” in the mechanical process they use to collect and distribute snow.

Single-stage snow blowers have an auger that pulls the snow into a large intake at the front of the snow blower, and propels it out of a chute mounted to the top of the machine. Single-stage blowers, also frequently referred to as “snow throwers,” are small, lightweight and easy to maneuver, making them ideal for clearing light snowfall and smaller driveways and walks.

Dual-stage snow blowers, as the name suggests, have a two-stage process for collecting and expelling snow. Like single-stage models, they have an auger that pulls snow into the intake. The dual-stage snow blower follows up by pushing the snow into an impeller that ejects it out through the chute.

The one-two punch of auger and impeller allows a two-stage snow blower to remove more snow quicker, and throw it a longer distance. That makes them perfect for large driveways. That said, they are larger and heavier than single-stage machines, so they may not be able to maneuver around narrow walking paths as easily.

The width and depth of a snow blower’s intake determine how much snow it can move with each pass, and thus, how long it takes you to get the job done. Most single-stage electric snow blowers have a clearing width of around 20 inches and a clearing depth of around 8 inches. That’s good for carving out walks and medium-sized areas. Some heavy-duty two-stage electric snow blowers can remove a 24-inch-wide and 20-inch-deep swath of snow, which will make quick work of a large driveway.

Throwing distance refers to how far a snow blower can launch snow out of the chute. This gives you a sense of how to plan when and how you’ll dispose of the snow in your path. The average single-stage snow blower typically has a short throwing distance—around 25 feet. Unsurprisingly, a two-stage snow blower can send its snow as far as 50 feet.

Snow blowers typically have a throttle that allows you to change their mechanical speed, which will adjust how far it throws your snow. There are also controls that allow you to rotate the chute to change the direction of the flow of snow. If you can map out your snow-blowing route, check and make sure your snow blower throws the snow far enough to keep it out of your way until it melts.

Most electric snow blowers receive power from multiple large rechargeable batteries, which allow them to produce nearly as much power as a gas snow blower. No battery supplies uninterrupted power for as long as a tank of gas, though: On average, you should expect a battery-powered snow blower to run for about 30 to 45 minutes on a single charge. You can extend that time if you have multiple batteries, but the low run time still caps how much ground they can cover.

Though we largely consider them to be obsolete, some manufacturers also still produce corded electric snow blowers, which plug into a standard electrical outlet. They’re often cheaper than battery-powered models and run as long as you need them to. However, having a power cord substantially reduces their range: You will likely need to purchase an extension cord to extend its reach slightly beyond the length of the area you need to clear. No matter how much slack you have, though, the cable makes the whole process a little more awkward.

“Cordless snow blowers are easier, better, and safer to use,” says Popular Mechanics Test Editor Brad Ford. “Corded is old, out-of-date tech in most cases.”

They’re also limited to smaller, 15-amp motors that run on the power an outlet can provide. That usually translates to narrower clearing widths, shallower clearing depths, and shorter throw distances. Unless you have a very tight budget, we highly recommend going with a battery-powered electric snow blower rather than a corded one.

The most important thing you can do to keep your electric snow blower running season after season is to simply make sure that you store your charger and batteries indoors when you aren’t charging or using them. Lithium cells aren't able to hold the same amount of charge when the temperature drops below freezing. By storing and charging those batteries indoors, you’ll get the most run time out of them.

If you use a corded snow blower, you shouldn’t plug it into any old extension cord. These machines draw a lot of power, and not every cord can handle it. Using the wrong one can create a fire hazard or damage your snow blower. Make sure to check your snow blower’s specs before buying an extension cord to pair with it, so you can be sure it can handle its amperage.

Most corded electric snow blowers have a 12-amp rating, in which case you’ll want a 12-gauge extension cord that can provide at least 12 amps of power. You’ll also want to make sure it’s long enough for you to reach the far end of whatever walkway or road you plan to clear, preferably with some slack to spare for maneuverability. We recommend starting with 100 feet and scaling up based on your property.

Regardless, it would be wise to buy an extension cord to match the specs you need for your snow blower, rather than using one that you happen to have lying around.

With advancements in battery technology, there are now powerful two-stage cordless snow blowers capable of clearing deeper, heavier snow.

That said, the most powerful electric snow blowers still don’t match the snow-moving capabilities of the largest gas-powered snow blowers on the market. The most powerful electric snow blowers work best at maximum depths of about a foot, while some gas-powered models can clear snow up to 2 feet deep.

Archaeologists have found the remains of a 2,900-year-old sanctuary on an island mountaintop, where ancient Greeks may have worshipped the goddess Artemis.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The discovery of a 2,900-year-old mountaintop sanctuary on a Mediterranean island shows the ancient Greek veneration for high mountains and their link to the Greek gods, archaeologists say.

The sanctuary was found during new excavations on Euboea, a very large island only about 30 miles (50 kilometers) northeast of Athens. The sanctuary did not include any buildings, such as a temple. Archaeologists think it was used for offerings and feasting by worshippers for hundreds of years, from about the ninth century B.C. until the first or second century A.D., during Imperial Roman times.

"We know that in the ancient Greek world, religious life was not limited to large temples and urban sanctuaries," excavation leader Chloé Chezeaux, an archaeologist at the Swiss School of Archeology in Greece, told Live Science in an email. "There were also many places of worship in the countryside and in the mountains."

Chezeaux led the excavations this year near the summit of Elatias, one of the highest peaks of Mount Olympus on Euboea. It is not, however, the mainland Mount Olympus traditionally regarded as the abode of the Greek gods.

Chezeaux said that her team first spotted signs of the sanctuary during an archaeological survey in 2025. In excavations throughout Greece, "mountaintop sanctuaries are not uncommon," she said. "The problem is that these sanctuaries often left very little archaeological evidence, sometimes with no visible structures at all, which makes them particularly difficult to identify."

Archaeologists found the sanctuary during a survey in 2025 and first excavated it in 2026.

The sanctuary on the Euboean Olympus, however, has yielded "an exceptional concentration of pottery," she said. The earliest is from at least the ninth century B.C., during the early Greek Geometric period — named after the distinctive patterns on ceramics of the time.

"This means that people were coming to this summit over several centuries, perhaps even for more than a thousand years," Chezeaux said.

The sanctuary was used in ancient times mainly by people from the nearby city of Eretria, where the Swiss School of Archaeology is now based.

"Reaching the summit is quite a physical challenge even today," Chezeaux said. "The final part of our ascent involves walking about 3 kilometres [1.8 miles], with an elevation gain of 650 metres [2,130 feet]"

Researchers now reach the summit from the nearest mountain pass in about an hour, but "it's difficult to estimate how long the journey would have taken in antiquity," she said. "Travel conditions were different, we don't know which routes people followed, and … not everyone visiting the sanctuary necessarily came from the city of Eretria."

The effort required to get to the mountaintop is part of the mystery.

"People were willing to devote considerable time and energy to reaching these places, and in our case they seem to have done so over many generations," Chezeaux said. This raised questions of what the mountain meant to worshippers, and why this particular summit remained important for so long, she said.

The immortal Greek gods of ancient myths were said to watch the affairs of mortal humans from their home on the summit of a different Mount Olympus, in a mountain range between the northern Greek regions of Thessaly and Macedonia. The highest mountain in Greece, it stands at over 9,500 feet (2,900 m) high, while the Euboean Olympus is almost 3,800 feet (1,100 m) high, and the Elatias peak on it is about 100 feet (30 m) lower than its highest peak.

The Mount Olympus in northern Greece is the highest of several mountains with that name.

The tradition of the northern Olympus on mainland Greece dates from the poems of Homer and Hesiod, which were written in about the eighth century B.C. But the name Olympus was already widespread for high mountains, and modern Greece has several mountains bearing this name.

Chezeaux said religious ceremonies were often held at the sanctuary high on the Euboean Olympus, as well as at other sites on the island.

"In antiquity, Eretria had a very rich religious life, with sanctuaries both within the city and throughout its territory," Chezeaux said. "Mount Olympus dominates much of the surrounding region, and its prominent position probably played a role in the choice of this location."

High mountains held particular significance for the ancient Greeks, and the journey to reach the sanctuary may have been part of the religious experience, she noted.

The excavation team has yet to find an altar at the sanctuary. While the chief Greek god Zeus is traditionally associated with mountaintops, an inscription at an ancient site in Eretria mentions "Artemis Olympia" — an epithet that suggests the wild nature goddess Artemis was worshipped at the mountaintop sanctuary.

The remains of offerings found in crevices at the site include bones from sheep and goats.

"Several of them show signs of burning, sometimes at very high temperatures," Chezeaux said. "These finds naturally suggest practices involving animal sacrifice and ritual meals, which played an important role in ancient Greek religion."

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6264. How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

North Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for new member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ said David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

But the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown said, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”

Womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic issues. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

“There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”

Womack said her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis said. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

“I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a new map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

“North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”

#6263. The 6 Best Remote Control Cars for Car-Loving Kids (And Kids at Heart)

Satisfy your need for speed, scaling, and off-roading with these fast, off-road-ready RC cars.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Some toys are timeless. From monster trucks that power over boulders to speed demons that clock 70 miles per hour, RC cars can thrill anyone who gets a controller in their hand for hours on end. Whether you’re an experienced driver looking to splurge on a higher-end model, a beginner looking for a new hobby, or a parent just trying to get your kid off the iPad, remote control cars are a great toy for all ages.

If you’re new to the RC world, shopping for a car (or an RC airplane, boat, or truck, for that matter) may feel somewhat daunting at first. It can get surprisingly technical, especially if you're looking at the hobby-grade cars. It helps to, at the very least, know how to tell the difference between the cars made for competitive racing and off-roading, detail-oriented models for collectors, and the more affordable options for kids and beginners. The good news is that while there may be a bit of a learning curve, you can get a taste of the action no matter your budget.

For more great toys kids of all ages are sure to love, check out our picks for the best remote control toys, the best drones, and the best robot toys.

Our testing focused on key features that factor into an RC car's day-to-day use, including speed, power, battery life, and handling. We drove a collection of cars on both flat indoor surfaces in our office, over uneven, hilly outdoor areas in New York’s Central Park, and through the fall foliage and around a tree-lined backyard in upstate New York. In addition to the basics, we measured the cars' acceleration, how quickly each car responded to radio signals, and checked the range of the remotes. We also took general notes on how easy it was to get the cars up and running.

There are two models on this list we haven't tested: the Bezgar Off-Road Monster Truck and the Tamiya Nismo R34 GT-R Z-Tune. We recommended them after reviewing user recommendations and enthusiast reviews to find cars that represented certain areas our test units didn't fill. Our research spanned a range of different vehicle types from reputable RC brands, including Traxxas, Laegendary, Redcat Racing, and Bezgar.

Across the board, we wanted to make sure this list represented a wide range of RC cars, including options at several price points. Our picks include toy cars that cost $50 or less, mid-range RC cars under $200, and a few pricey models for experienced adult enthusiasts that cost as much as $350.

In our latest update, we performed additional testing on our existing recommendations, as well as a few new cars. We also removed one recommendation, the VR Real Racer, as it has been out of stock for several months.

The Traxxas Stampede RC car is our top choice because it combines speed, handling, and power better than any other option we tested. Its oversized monster truck tires aren’t just for show: They provided great traction and grip on dirt and rocks, as well as concrete and linoleum. Even compared to more speed-focused cars, the Traxxas brings some notable zip.

What impressed us most, though, was the handling. Even on uneven grass and dirt, we felt comfortable making sharp turns and precise movements at high speeds and the vehicle didn’t topple over. And it handled crashes like a champ: It took a few accidental head-on collisions into trees and fell as much as three feet off some rocks in the park and was no worse for wear.

Another key distinction for this RC car was how responsive and powerful the suspension was. Driving on bumpy surfaces and through dirt never swayed or threw it off course. The suspension made it easier to perform short jumps over ramps and ledges without crashing or damaging the vehicle.

This well-priced off-road monster truck has working roll bar headlights, a spare tire attached to the back chassis, and an aluminum body that handles collisions at the truck’s top speed of 12 miles per hour. Its feature-rich design is an excellent value for beginners and experienced RCers alike.

The two-wheel-drive remote-control car is on the smaller side, at 1/14th scale, but it has a powerful motor to keep it rolling for up to 20 minutes on its all-terrain tires. The 2.4 GHz remote works from a distance of more than 160 feet away.

While it isn't quite as powerful or durable as our top pick, it serves as a perfect on-ramp to hobby-grade RC, giving you more oomph than a cheap toy.

If you’ve got a love for model cars, this is the right RC car for you. This scaled-down Ford Bronco is the near spitting image of the real thing, minus the less-than-ideal gas mileage. This miniature has grippy tires that match its slow but powerful motor. Just like the real thing, this Bronco climbs over rocks and rallies up inclines with ease.

We tested the car going up large boulders in the park, and while it never zoomed over them, it continued moving effortlessly. We, of course, love the accurate exterior shell, but also found the interior body to be quite impressive.

The TRX-4M has a flexible frame and suspension system that allows for easy climbing on uneven surfaces. It comes with two headlights which, when the Bronco shell is snapped on, only further adds to the look.

You can grab one of these RC cars in multiple colors, including blue, orange, white, red, and black.

If you want speed, try out this LaTrax Desert Prerunner racing truck. While it may not win you any competitive RC races with professional builds, this is a hobby-grade car with some serious juice behind it for its size. Driving it around required a bit of adjustment time because of its quick acceleration and sharp turning radius, but that’s exactly the type of challenge we love to tackle.

The grippy tires and bouncy suspension also meant that this car picks up some serious speed outdoors. We drove it over hills and through rocks without losing any speed in the process. We loved the way it spins and drifts when it has some dirt or gravel underneath it and found ourselves trying to spin it around trees for fun.

The car, much like other Traxxas products, is also quite durable. It handled a few spills and wipeouts with no real damage to the body or motor. That said, be careful driving it through leaves and sticks because we found several accumulated under the outer shell after our drive.

Many of the RC cars we tested are off-roaders with thick tires, grippy treads, and bouncy suspensions. This allows them to drive quickly and responsively across tons of different surfaces like dirt, gravel, grass, and up rocks. This model from Tamiya is designed for the exact opposite: It features slick, smooth tires and a low-profile design that's built for outdoor or indoor play on hard surfaces like tile or hardwood.

This is because the remote control car is built for one thing and one thing only: drifting. Just like stunt drivers on a movie set, these cars spin and slide across the ground for cinematic turns and stylish maneuvering.

Bear in mind, however, that this car does not come ready to race. This is an assembly kit that requires patience, steady hands, and additional materials like glue and a hobby knife. Furthermore, the car will also require an electronic speed controller (ESC), battery, and radio receiver.

If you aren't ready to commit to full-size model, this tiny RC car from Hot Wheels fits in the palm of your hand, and has an equally miniature price tag. While it doesn't have the speed or torque of the larger models on this list, this is a perfect way to introduce young kids to the thrill of remote control driving.

The mini Lambo, a 1/16th scale model, is also perfect gift for sports car lovers looking for a bit of fun. The RC car is built with a rechargeable battery already in the body. So, whenever it needs to be charged up, plug the cable directly into the car.

The mini size is more for just convenience, too. The car is designed to fit and drive on all the same Hot Wheels tracks that work for the classic die cast models the brand is known for. So, if you already have a Hot Wheels enthusiast in mind, this is a great addition to their collection.

Based on our testing, the biggest distinction between RC cars is that some are hobby-grade models for racing or off-roading hobbyists, and others are beginner-friendly toys that are usually made for kids and beginners.

Hobby-grade RC cars come with powerful motors, beefy batteries, and the torque and speed to handle outdoor driving over tough terrain or competitive racing. These are typically more expensive than their toy counterparts and are better suited for buyers who want to seriously dive into RC cars or are already major fans. Toy RC cars are slower and get less run time per charge, but are much more affordable.

RC cars also come in a wide variety of builds, including off-road 4x4s and buggies, rock crawlers (built for more rigid, extreme off-roading), and drift cars (best for turns and speed). You’ll often see the RC car’s scale listed, especially for model cars, representing its size in relation to the real deal.

While shopping, you may see the initials “RTR” in product descriptions, which stand for “ready to race.” This means you can start driving right out of the box or after charging, with no extra parts required to get it up and running. Cars may be labeled RTR even if the batteries are sold separately, though, so make sure to check the packaging.

Speed varies depending on what the car is built to do. For example, rock climbers don’t have to be incredibly fast to tackle boulders, but they need powerful high-torque motors, whereas a race car should hit at least 20 to 30 miles per hour, depending on your level of competition. Before you buy, make sure you have in mind where you expect most of your RC driving to happen and what kind of features are important to you.

If you want a taste of everything, there are a number of cars that are in the middle ground, offering enough speed to make straightaways fun and enough power to handle grass, inclines, and some gravel.

Less expensive RC cars generally have a two-button remote control, and those on the higher end have 2.4 GHz (a speedy signal transmission speed) pistol-grip-style remotes with more advanced steering and throttles. These remotes are more responsive, allowing you to make quick turns, rapidly accelerate, or even reverse at a moment's notice. 2.4 GHz remote controls are what you’ll likely see in any hobby-grade RC cars. If you go for a high-end model, ensure that replacement parts and upgrades are readily available. Otherwise, you’ll have to search for outdated parts on eBay.

Quantinuum's Helios processor achieved a record-low failure rate of just 0.0005%, suggesting fault-tolerant quantum systems may need far fewer qubits than previously thought.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists at Quantinuum say they've set a new record in quantum error correction that brings large-scale, fault-tolerant systems one step closer.

The team claims their 98-qubit quantum system, Helios, demonstrated a failure rate of just 0.0005% in tests of its quantum memory, which is equivalent to an estimated five uncorrectable errors per million rounds of error checking.

This rate bests the previous benchmark set by Google's 105-qubit Willow quantum chip, which demonstrated an estimated 772 uncorrectable errors per million rounds in comparable tests, for an error rate of 0.0772%.

The result brings quantum computing closer to the "megaquop regime," where systems can run over a million operations without encountering an error, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study uploaded Oct. 16 to the arXiv preprint server.

In a statement, Robin Blume-Kohout, co-director of Sandia National Laboratories' Quantum Performance Lab, called the achievement "a significant milestone that quantum computing researchers have been working toward for many years."

"A scaled-up version of this system could reach the reliability required for useful fault-tolerant computation at a feasible size — less than a million physical qubits — which improves the outlook for practical quantum computing," added Blume-Kohout, who was not involved in the research.

Preserving the fragile information stored in qubits is one of quantum computing's greatest challenges and presents a major barrier to making systems practical.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Qubits, the most basic units of quantum information, are extremely sensitive to interference. Their delicate quantum states can be easily disturbed by heat, vibrations and other forms of environmental "noise," and if this happens in the middle of a calculation, the result becomes far less reliable — if it survives at all.

Quantum error correction has become a focal point for researchers for this exact reason. It introduces redundancy to quantum systems to ensure that small, potentially manageable errors don't wipe out entire calculations.

This involves spreading quantum information across multiple physical qubits to form a "logical" qubit. If a single qubit loses its quantum state due to interference, the redundancy provided by the logical qubit helps to keep the information it collectively stores intact.

The challenge is packing enough qubits into computers to ensure redundancy for longer, more complex calculations. This presents something of a catch-22: Adding more qubits provides more redundancy, allowing for larger quantum systems, but it also increases the opportunity for errors.

Unlike Google's Willow processor, which is based on superconducting circuits, Helios uses electrically charged barium ions that can be dynamically rearranged.

By shuttling ions around the processor, scientists can unite different pairs of qubits, allowing them to exchange information directly. That way, it doesn't have to pass through multiple qubits — a process that can introduce additional errors.

The team also developed a technique called "leakage repumping," which uses precise, split-second laser pulses to bring qubits that have slipped out of their information-storing quantum state back into a usable state.

To test how effectively Helios could correct errors as more physical qubits were added, the researchers used a type of error-correcting code known as a color code. They tested three progressively larger versions ‪—‬ known as code distances 3, 5 and 7 ​​—‬ which could correct one, two and three physical-qubit errors, respectively.

They found that Helios became substantially more reliable as they added more physical qubits. Each increase in code distance reduced the likelihood of an uncorrectable error by roughly 12 times. At the highest level tested (distance 7), Helios achieved a record failure rate of approximately one uncorrectable error per 200,000 rounds.

In the study, which has not been peer-reviewed yet, the scientists suggested that future quantum computers using the same technology as Helios could achieve extremely low error rates without needing an impractically high number of physical qubits.

According to estimates from Quantinuum representatives, a future trapped-ion system could support 100 logical qubits using approximately 30,000 physical qubits, compared with around 900,000 for a competing superconducting system.

"There is still substantial engineering ahead to scale to much larger systems and integrate all the elements of fault-tolerant computation, but this work demonstrates that our underlying hardware and error-correction approach can deliver the exponential improvement in reliability that large-scale quantum computers will depend upon," Dave Hayes, director of computational design and theory at Quantinuum, told Live Science in an email.

We’re constantly testing and writing about pocket knives here at Popular Mechanics, and Benchmade is a brand that always tops our list of favorites. Its folders, automatics, flippers, and fixed blades are beautifully designed using all high-quality materials, and all are U.S.-made in its Oregon headquarters. But there’s no denying they’re pricey, costing upward of $200, and they rarely go on sale for much of a discount.

But right now, ahead of Black Friday, Benchmade is knocking 20 percent off three of its most popular knives on Amazon—the Osborne, the Bugout, and the Bailout—for a savings of roughly $70 each.

When the Osborne debuted in 2000, it was Benchmade’s first blade to sport the Axis lock, which been replicated in some form by nearly every major knife manufacturer since its patent expired in 2019. It’s designed for ambidextrous operation and fast, one-handed deployment, plus it keeps your fingers clear of the blade while you open and close the knife.

This seasonal version uses CPM-S90V stainless super steel, which offers great edge retention and reliable toughness for everyday tasks like opening boxes. It’s coated with a protective distressed finish to make the reverse tanto-style blade look rustic and has a rich-looking dark-green aluminum handle, with copper accents. It feels good in hand—a durable yet lightweight EDC knife.

The Bugout is the knife our resident expert Justin Park grabs first for backpacking, camping and hunting and says it’s “arguably the defining pocket knife of the explosion of modern EDC blades.” It’s strong, but ultra lightweight and hardly registers in your pocket or pack.

Like the Osborne above, the Bugout uses S90V stainless super steel, featuring a shorter drop-point blade, copper accents, and handle that combines the same dark-green aluminum with a grippy and rugged-looking canvas micarta.

The Bailout is lightweight and tough. It has a longer drop-point tanto-style S90V stainless steel blade covered in the same stonewashed protective finish as the Bugout and Osborne, along with the same dark-green aluminum handle and copper accents. While it’s another great choice for EDC, the Bailout is outfitted with tactical-style elements, like the lanyard slot at the rear and the deep-carry clip.

On Wednesday (Nov. 25), the distant ice giant Uranus will be at its best and brightest. Here's when, where and how to look for the seventh planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of the hardest planets to see in the solar system — the distant ice giant Uranus — reaches its annual opposition on Wednesday (Nov. 25), just a day after the Beaver Supermoon. It's the best time to see the seventh planet from the sun, but you'll need to use stargazing binoculars or a good backyard telescope to find it.

Uranus is faint, slow-moving and rarely a target for casual stargazers. However, on Nov. 25, and, for a few weeks on either side, it will be at its closest point to Earth this year and will appear at its brightest, making it possible to spot.

Opposition occurs when Earth passes between Uranus and the sun; Uranus will be "opposite" the sun, hence, "opposition." The moment of opposition will happen at 6 p.m. ET on Nov. 25, according to EarthSky. Consequently, Uranus will rise in the east around sunset, reach its highest point in the sky around midnight and set in the west around sunrise.

You can find it in the constellation Taurus, close to the Pleiades open star cluster, also known as the Seven Sisters and M45. Uranus will be a few degrees southeast of the cluster, appearing as a faint point of light, about two-fifths of the distance between the Pleiades and Aldebaran, the brightest star in Taurus.

At magnitude +5.6, Uranus is technically visible to the naked eye under very dark skies. However, binoculars or a telescope will make it much easier to find.

Uranus as seen by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope.

At opposition, Uranus will be 18.4 astronomical units (AU) from Earth — about 1.7 billion miles (2.7 billion kilometers) away. Through a telescope, it will appear as a tiny blue-green disk. Its color comes from methane in its atmosphere, which absorbs red wavelengths of sunlight.

Named after Ouranos, the ancient Greek god of the sky and the heavens, according to the Planetary Society , Uranus is one of the least understood planets in the solar system. A day on Uranus lasts for about 17 hours, and the planet rotates sideways, according to NASA. It takes 84 Earth years to orbit the sun.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Uranus also has 13 faint rings and at least 29 known moons, the most recent of which was found in 2025 by the James Webb Space Telescope. It was named Uranus XXVIII and orbits between the moons Ophelia and Bianca. Many of Uranus' moons are named after characters from the works of William Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

The distant planet has been visited only once, by NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft on Jan. 24, 1986. However, contrary to what the probe found, scientists now think the planet emits its own internal heat. That could increase pressure on NASA to prepare a Uranus Orbiter and Probe (UOP), a mission concept the National Academy of Sciences recommended in 2022 as a high-priority planetary science mission for the next decade.

Uranus will next come to opposition on Nov. 30, 2027.

Jamie Carter is a Cardiff, U.K.-based freelance science journalist and a regular contributor to Live Science. He is the author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners and co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and leads international stargazing and eclipse-chasing tours. His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.
